docs.title: amplifactory
docs.text:
amplifactory turns a repository into an issue-driven agent factory. In a GitHub Copilot or Claude Code session (the orchestrator) you turn an idea into prioritized lanes of ordered GitHub issues. The factory then takes each issue to a merged PR: a builder plans, builds and fixes, a fresh reviewer checks, and the orchestrator merges when every gate passes. When it needs you, it asks on the PR and keeps working on other lanes.

It's a Copier template: one command creates a repo with the rules, the factory skill, CI, labels, branch protection and a Project board. copier update brings in later releases.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
• Quick start

    One small CLI, from copier copy of the template to a merged PR with CI on your Mac's runner pool.

    Quick start

  • Create a project

    Generate a repo from the template, then run bootstrap.sh for the GitHub side: labels, branch protection and the Project board.

    Create a project

  • Your first run

    Brainstorm into lanes, then say "run the factory" and watch the first issue go from plan to merge.

    Your first run

docs.title: What makes it work
docs.text: Idea In short Lanes and priorities Features become lanes of ordered sub-issues; P0–P3 and "blocked by" links set the schedule. The pipeline One builder and one fresh reviewer per issue. Before a first release only blockers are fixed in the PR; the rest become improvement issues. Flag and continue Questions go on the PR with options and a recommendation. Answer whenever you like, then say "resume". Real data never, with-approval or allowed: how far agents may read real data. It is never committed or quoted. Docs ship with the code Every code change brings its docs; the Handoff's Docs line is a merge gate. Lessons A factory problem found in your project becomes a lesson issue here, then a release, then an update in every project. Copilot and Claude Code Run the factory in either: setup, a model per role, what differs, and the Actions mode with each. Keep up to date sync-root-factory moves a repo to the latest release by PR; factory-lesson files factory problems in this repo. Local CI One runner pool per Mac runs the CI of every factory repo on it, where GitHub-hosted runners are off. Where knowledge lives Issues, PRs, review threads, plans and Handoffs are the source of truth; the run log (.factory/runs/) and agent memory only point at them.

docs.title: The GitHub Actions mode
docs.text: Optional: agents run on GitHub Actions when you add labels. No session of yours is needed, but it is slower than the skill. The agents are the GitHub Copilot CLI (signed in with each workflow's own token) or Claude Code GitHub Actions (needs a Claude subscription and the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN secret).

docs.title: Turning it on or off
docs.text:
Copier's actions_agent question decides which workflows are rendered:

actions_agent What the repo gets none (default for a new project) No factory-*.yml workflows; you run the factory with the skill. copilot Design, build, review and the label guard, with the Copilot CLI (below); the README's "Actions mode with Copilot (optional)". claude The five workflows below; the README's "Actions mode with Claude (optional)". 
uvx copier copy --data actions_agent=copilot gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory my-project   # a new project with it
uvx copier update --data actions_agent=copilot   # add it, or switch agents, in a PR of its own
uvx copier update --data actions_agent=none      # remove it

A project generated before the question existed keeps its workflows; copier update (or sync-root-factory) defaults the question to claude. The model is agent_model with claude (default sonnet) and copilot_model with copilot (default claude-sonnet-5.5; any model your plan offers), for example --data agent_model=opus. Each is asked only with its agent.

issue ──(you: factory:design)──► DESIGN agent ──► draft design PR
                                                      │  you review; edit it, or "@claude revise …"
                              (you: design:approved) ─┘
                                                      ▼
                     BUILD agent on factory/issue-N: implement, run checks until green, open PR
                                                      ▼
                     REVIEW agent: PR vs. approved design + CLAUDE.md
                                                      ▼
                                              you merge
Workflow Runs when factory-design.yml you add factory:design to an issue factory-build.yml you add design:approved to a design PR factory-review.yml a build PR opens or updates; with Copilot, also on demand (gh workflow run factory-review.yml -f pr=N) factory-chat.yml claude only: you write @claude on an issue or PR factory-label-guard.yml anyone but you adds a trigger label: it's removed

docs.title: With Copilot
docs.text:
• No secret. Each workflow asks for copilot-requests: write; its GITHUB_TOKEN signs in the CLI. Requests bill the repo owner's Copilot seat.
  • Runners. Jobs go to your Mac's runner pool when FACTORY_RUNNER is local and the repo is private, otherwise to ubuntu-latest. In an internal repo where GitHub-hosted runners are off, the agent jobs wait in the queue: don't use this mode there. The pool is no security boundary (agent shell commands run as you), which is why it serves only repos where just you and your collaborators can write issues and comments.
  • Prompts. The agents run /design-issue N, /build-from-design N and /review-against-design PR from .claude/commands/, with --model set to copilot_model. Each job installs a pinned Copilot CLI (@github/copilot@1.0.116) with auto-update off.
  • Workflows may open pull requests. Bootstrap turns on "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" (Settings → Actions → General); without it the design and build agents can't open PRs. A copier update that adds the mode prints the command to run: gh api -X PUT repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/permissions/workflow -F can_approve_pull_request_reviews=true.
  • A missing PR fails the run. The design and build jobs check that their PR is open and turn red if not, unless the agent marked the issue factory:blocked and commented why.
  • No chat. There's no @-mention workflow: edit the design branch yourself.

docs.title: Approving the PR's runs
docs.text:
GitHub holds the pull_request runs (CI, review) of a PR that a workflow token opens until someone approves them, and a workflow_dispatch CI run doesn't count as the required check. So factory-build's second job, approve-runs, approves them. It has actions: write (the only job that does) and runs no agent.

  • It takes only a same-repo factory/issue-N PR into the default branch. Any other PR, or a second open PR from the branch, turns it red.
  • It approves until three lists, 10 s apart, add no runs, for at most 3 minutes, then warns you to approve any run still held.
  • gh workflow run factory-review.yml -f pr=N runs the review on demand, on a same-repo factory/issue-N PR only.

docs.title: Tool rules
docs.text:
Before each agent starts, its job installs a preToolUse hook, .github/factory/tool_rules.py, copied from the default branch (never from a checkout an agent can write). It denies:

  • a shell command outside the stage's allowlist (the design agent may run gh pr create but no other gh pr command; the build agent may run uv run --no-sync pytest and the pinned uvx ruff@…, not uv add);
  • anything its small bash reader doesn't model: $, backticks, redirections, globs, subshells, background jobs (a heredoc with a quoted delimiter is fine);
  • writes by the design agent outside .factory/designs/, and all writes by the review agent;
  • gh pr merge for every agent, gh pr review for the build agent, approving or requesting changes for the review agent. gh pr flags go after the subcommand.

The job stops before the agent if the hook is missing or doesn't deny. Change it only in a reviewed PR.

docs.title: Only your approval merges
docs.text: .github/CODEOWNERS is * @you and bootstrap's "Protect main" ruleset requires a code owner's review, so no token, bot or collaborator can approve a PR into a merge. Your own PRs, the skill's included, merge with the ruleset's admin bypass (--admin). Without that ruleset nothing enforces this, and bootstrap warns. Use the Actions mode only for repos whose issue text you control.

docs.title: GitHub quirks it works around
docs.text:
• A PR that changes a workflow skips that workflow's stage (Claude). With Copilot, agents can't push workflow changes at all. Put workflow changes in their own PR.
  • PR runs use the merge ref from the PR's last update. After a merge, click Update branch on open PRs, or they run old workflows.
  • PRs authored by claude[bot] need allowed_bots and the right restrict_untrusted_prs setting, or the review job is green but does nothing (Claude).

docs.title: Using both
docs.text: The skill and the Actions mode share .claude/commands/ and CLAUDE.md. The skill never adds trigger labels or writes @claude, and works on local/issue-N branches while the Actions review only takes factory/issue-*, so they don't start each other. Pick one per issue. If you only use the skill, remove the Actions mode with uvx copier update --data actions_agent=none, or turn single workflows off with gh workflow disable <workflow>.

docs.title: The hard rule
docs.text: A CLAUDE.md hard rule: every code change brings its documentation in the same PR: new docs for new behaviour, and updates to any README, CHANGELOG, docstring or .factory/designs/ text the change makes wrong. A PR whose docs disagree with its code is a blocker, even in mvp.

docs.title: The Handoff's Docs line and its gate
docs.text: The PR body's Handoff has a Docs line naming the docs updated, or "none needed" with a reason that holds up (required when code changes but docs don't). This is merge gate 12: no Docs line, no merge. The reviewer also checks that docs and code agree in the changed area.

docs.title: Documentation tech-debt
docs.text:
A docs mismatch that existed before the PR isn't fixed in it. The reviewer tags it doc-debt, and the orchestrator files it as a sub-issue of the repo's "Documentation tech-debt" tracking issue (labels documentation, P2; each todo documentation, improvement, P2). Documentation todos that come up while planning go there too, never as loose issues.

lanes.py doc-debt manages the tracker (python3 .claude/skills/factory/scripts/lanes.py doc-debt ...):

Command What it does find Prints the tracking issue's number, creating it if missing. add Files a doc todo (or links an existing issue) as a sub-issue. list Lists open todos (number and title), for the builder's ride-alongs.

Ride-alongs: the plan step pastes the open todos into the plan. When the PR already touches a file a todo is about, the builder fixes that too and the PR says Closes #<todo>. It never opens other files just for doc-debt.

bootstrap.sh creates the tracking issue; in older repos doc-debt find creates it on first use.

docs.title: Flag and continue
docs.text: The factory doesn't stop the run to wait for you unless nothing else can proceed.

docs.title: When it asks
docs.text:
• A plan or review raises a question only you can answer (scope, an interface, a dependency, a data source).
  • A gate fails and the fix isn't mechanical.
  • The orchestrator is unsure whether to merge (gate 13).
  • More lanes are ready than you've allowed (asked once, in the session).

docs.title: How it asks
docs.text:
1. An inline review comment tagged [question], with options and a recommendation.
  2. The label factory:needs-maintainer on the PR.
  3. The run log records it as asked, with a link to the thread.
  4. Only that lane pauses. Other lanes carry on.

docs.title: How you answer
docs.text:
Reply in the thread on GitHub, whenever you like. Then, in Copilot or Claude Code:

resume the factory

queue.py lists the lane as replied, ahead of new work. The orchestrator applies your answer (via the builder), resolves the thread, removes the label and continues to the gates.

docs.title: Ready to merge
docs.text:
A refused merge is not a question, so it doesn't get factory:needs-maintainer. When every gate passes but the merge is refused (the harness denies gh pr merge, or GitHub rejects it; in Copilot that includes a "No" at the approval prompt and a denial in autopilot or a -p run), the factory:

  1. labels the PR and issue factory:ready-to-merge and removes the in-progress label;
  2. posts one PR comment: the exact merge command and the gate summary;
  3. moves on. The issue stays open, so its lane's later issues wait.

It never works around the refusal. queue.py lists these under "Waiting for you to merge", and the end-of-run report lists them so you can merge in one batch.

docs.title: Let the factory merge
docs.text:
Opt in with a permission rule. The template doesn't ship one.

Claude Code. Add this to the repo's .claude/settings.json or your user ~/.claude/settings.json:

{ "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(gh pr merge * --merge --admin --delete-branch)"] } }
  • The rule lets the agent use your ruleset bypass.
  • It matches only commands ending in --delete-branch, which is how the skill runs the merge (gates.md "Merge"); variants with -R or other trailing flags aren't covered.
  • A project rule applies only after you accept the workspace trust prompt.
  • For how allow rules interact with auto mode, see the permissions and permission modes docs, and try it in your own session.

GitHub Copilot. The rule above does nothing: Copilot doesn't read permissions from .claude/settings.json, and its own rules can't single out the merge (--allow-tool='shell(gh pr)', or "Yes, and don't ask again" on a gh pr merge prompt, approves every gh pr command, gh pr close included). Use a personal hook that runs the skill's merge_hook.py (scripts). It approves only gh pr merge <N> --merge [--admin] --delete-branch, typed exactly so, and leaves every other request to the normal prompt.

  1. Copy the script out of the repo, so no branch or file edit can change what it approves. Copy it again after a factory update.
mkdir -p ~/.copilot/hooks && cp .claude/skills/factory/scripts/merge_hook.py ~/.copilot/hooks/

On Windows, in PowerShell:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force ~/.copilot/hooks | Out-Null; Copy-Item .claude/skills/factory/scripts/merge_hook.py ~/.copilot/hooks/
  1. Save this as ~/.copilot/hooks/factory-merge.json. If you set COPILOT_HOME, Copilot reads personal hooks from $COPILOT_HOME/hooks/ instead, so put both files there.
{ "version": 1, "hooks": { "permissionRequest": [ { "type": "command", "matcher": "bash|powershell", "timeoutSec": 10,
  "bash": "test -f \"$COPILOT_HOOK_DIR/merge_hook.py\" && python3 \"$COPILOT_HOOK_DIR/merge_hook.py\" || true",
  "powershell": "$f = Join-Path $env:COPILOT_HOOK_DIR 'merge_hook.py'; if (Test-Path $f) { [Console]::In.ReadToEnd() | python $f }; exit 0" } ] } }
  • The bash command runs on macOS and Linux, the powershell one on Windows (as python; use py if that's how Python runs there).
  • It applies in every repo you use Copilot in, for that one command. A missing script or any error falls back to the normal prompt, and a merge that is still refused is handed off.
  • Don't commit it as a repository hook (.github/hooks/): that would run the working tree's copy of the script, which any file edit could turn into an allow-all.
  • See the Copilot hooks reference.

docs.title: What never happens
docs.text:
• The skill never adds the Actions-mode trigger labels (factory:design, design:approved) and never writes @claude. Those would start GitHub Actions agents.
  • The factory never merges PRs that change .github/, CLAUDE.md or .claude/. You merge those.

docs.title: Lanes and priorities
docs.text:
A lane is a feature one builder can carry from start to finish: a parent issue labelled lane, whose native sub-issues, in order, are the lane's issues.

Lane A: STS end-to-end (P0)      #4 ──► #6
Lane B: ConvoMem datasets (P1)   #5 ──► #8 ──► #9
Lane C: OpenRouter traces (P2)   #7
Lane D: Hardening (P3)           #17 ──► #18 ──► … ──► #25     (blocked by lane A)

docs.title: The rules
docs.text: Rule Within a lane Strictly in order, one issue at a time. The current issue is the first open sub-issue; when it merges, the next becomes current. Across lanes Ranked by priority. One lane at a time by default; when more are ready, the skill asks once whether to run them in parallel. Priority Exactly one label: P0 must have now, P1 next, P2 later, P3 someday or hardening. No label counts as P2. Dependencies Native "blocked by" links, between issues or whole lanes. A "Depends on #N" line in the body is read as a fallback. Questions A question on a lane's PR pauses only that lane. A paused lane uses no slot, so the next lane may start. Merges Always one at a time.

docs.title: The main path
docs.text: Every brainstorm names a main path: the smallest chain of issues that makes the thing work end to end. It's a P0 lane. Polish and hardening go in a low-priority lane.

docs.title: Rolling-wave detail
docs.text: Only the next one or two issues per lane are written in full. Later ones are stubs (title, one-line goal, dependencies) detailed when they come close.

docs.title: Parallel lanes
docs.text:
With --lanes N, up to N lanes are active at once, each with its own worktree and builder.

  • Before a second lane starts, a collision guard compares its plan's "Files & interfaces touched" with the files the other active lane is changing, and holds it if they overlap.
  • After each merge, the other active lanes' branches are updated with main before their review.

docs.title: Proposals become issues
docs.text: Work the orchestrator proposes becomes issues, not an ad-hoc fix. This covers audit results, recommended follow-ups and fixes it would offer at the end of a turn or in the final report. It proposes a sub-issue of the lane that fits, a new lane if none does, or a doc-debt sub-issue, naming the lane, title and priority. One confirmation creates them with gh issue create, wired with lanes.py, and the work goes through the queue. Findings inside a run keep their routes (improvement issues, doc-debt, PR questions). Problems in the factory template repo are lesson issues (the factory-lesson skill).

docs.title: Seeing it
docs.text:
• python3 .claude/skills/factory/scripts/queue.py prints the lanes, each lane's current issue and state (active, replied, ready, asked, blocked, waiting, done), and "Work now".
  • The Project board created by bootstrap.sh: group by Parent issue for each lane with a progress bar; sort by Priority.
  • scripts/lanes.py creates and reorders lanes, sub-issues, dependencies and priorities.

docs.title: What counts
docs.text:
A lesson is about the factory, not your project's code:

  • a default, question or message in the template that was wrong or misleading;
  • a skill step, brief or gate that made an agent do the wrong thing, or blocked a good PR;
  • a script (queue.py, lanes.py, bootstrap.sh, the runner pool) that failed on realistic input.

A bug in your project is an ordinary issue in your project.

docs.title: File it when it happens
docs.text:
Say it in the session where you hit it:

file a factory lesson: the builder skipped the Docs line in the Handoff

The factory-lesson skill finds the template from _src_path in .copier-answers.yml, searches the lesson issues for a duplicate, drafts the body (what happened with links, the fix you applied in the project, the template files to change), checks it for real data, secrets and private paths, and asks you once. It files in the template's repo. It never files in your project. How it picks the repo: Keep up to date.

Fix the problem in your project first if you can: the lesson records the fix, so the template change is small.

docs.title: How it reaches you
docs.text:
1. A release PR (release/vX.Y.Z) closes the lessons it fixes and adds a changelog entry for each. See Evolving the template.
  2. After the tag, say "sync the factory to the latest release" in your project. sync-root-factory opens a PR with the update; you merge it. Or run uvx copier update. See Keep up to date.

A lesson the template already fixed is answered with the fixing release and the update command, not a new issue.

docs.title: Local CI
docs.text:
Some accounts can't use GitHub-hosted runners (EMU personal repos, for one), so a generated repo's CI never starts. The runner pool runs that CI on your Mac instead: one pool per Mac, serving every factory repo on it, with a fresh runner for each job.

Do you need it? Only when GitHub-hosted runners are off for your account. The setup is opt-in: say "set up CI runners", or set FACTORY_RUNNER=local, and "run the factory" then checks the pool each time. Otherwise skip this page.

With the repo variable FACTORY_RUNNER=local, the generated ci.yml asks for runs-on: [self-hosted, factory-run-<run_id>] (CI variables). The pool, a login service on your Mac, watches the queue of each registered repo and, for each queued job:

  1. asks GitHub for a just-in-time runner with exactly those two labels;
  2. starts it in a fresh copy of its base install (or in a container, see below);
  3. lets it take that one job, then deletes it and logs one line to jobs.jsonl.

At most slots runners run at once. Free slots are shared fairly across repos, then across pull requests (P0 first). Runs from forks never run locally.

docs.title: Operate the pool
docs.text:
R=.claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/runners.py
python3 $R status                              # up, paused or down; slots; the queue
python3 $R pause --reason "a demo at 3"        # no new runners; running jobs finish
python3 $R resume
python3 $R stats --days 7                      # waits and run times, p50 and p95
python3 $R logs --run 123456                   # a run's runner logs
python3 $R config --slots 6 --battery half     # capacity; half the slots on battery

status makes no API call. Its exit code is 0 when up, 5 when paused and 3 when down (no heartbeat for 2 minutes). By default the pool leaves your Mac 4 performance cores and 16 GB of RAM, at about 2 GB per slot, and starts nothing while memory pressure is critical. Runners run at low priority, and the pool keeps the Mac awake while any runner is alive.

docs.title: Container mode (optional)
docs.text:
Each job runs in its own Linux container (ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner, Ubuntu 24.04) instead of on your Mac as you. It needs Docker Desktop, with about 2 GB of Docker's VM per slot.

S=.claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/setup.py
python3 $S container check              # Docker, and its VM's size
python3 $S container on --yes           # pulls the image, restarts the pool
python3 $S container off --yes          # new jobs run on the Mac again

It covers the whole pool. Docker must be running, jobs start cold, and jobs that need Docker (services:, container:) fail. The Actions mode with Copilot's agent jobs don't run in containers yet: keep the pool on the Mac while a repo uses that mode.

docs.title: Security in one paragraph
docs.text: On the Mac, a job runs as you. Use the pool only for your own private repos. A job gets its own HOME, a short environment allowlist and no GH_TOKEN, so your logins aren't picked up by accident, but that is not a boundary: it can read your files. Container mode keeps your files and logins out of reach. Details: Runner pool details.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text: The pool home is ~/.amplifactory/runner-pool/ ($FACTORY_RUNNER_POOL_HOME overrides it): config.json, logs/, jobs.jsonl, heartbeat.json, paused.json while paused, and shared caches in cache/. The login service is com.amplifactory.runner-pool. To remove everything: python3 .claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/setup.py service uninstall --purge --yes.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
The skill runs in your GitHub Copilot or Claude Code session, the orchestrator: it picks work, checks plans, verifies findings and merges. Subagents do the heavy lifting.

Role Default model (Claude Code / Copilot) Lifetime Does Orchestrator opus / claude-opus-5.5 (your session) the run queue, plan check, gates, merge, run log Builder sonnet / claude-sonnet-5.5 one per issue, reused for build and fixes plan → build → fixes, keeps the PR's Handoff current Design reviewer opus / claude-opus-5.5, fresh critical issues only reviews the plan before any code Code reviewer opus / claude-opus-5.5, fresh once per issue inline findings while CI runs

Change the models in the generated CLAUDE.md ("Models"). The skill's "Claude Code and Copilot" table maps each action onto the harness's tools: the builder is reused with SendMessage in Claude Code, and in Copilot it is a background agent messaged with write_agent.

  1. Plan. The builder writes .factory/designs/issue-N.md (goal, approach, files and interfaces touched, dependencies, risks, tests) and opens a draft PR from local/issue-N.
  2. Plan check. Standard issues: you read the plan. Critical issues (privacy or security code, a new dependency, a shared data contract, a public interface others build on) get a fresh design reviewer.
  3. Build. The same builder implements, updates the affected docs, runs the checks from CLAUDE.md until green, fills in the PR's Handoff (including a Docs line: what was updated, or "none needed" and why) and marks it ready.
  4. Review ∥ CI. A fresh reviewer checks the diff against the plan and CLAUDE.md, including that docs and code agree (see Docs ship with the code). It posts inline comments tagged [blocker], [improvement], [doc-debt] or [question]; every blocker comes with a reproduction.
  5. Fix. The builder fixes blockers. You verify each with its reproduction on the new commit and resolve the thread. There is no second full review.
  6. Gates and merge. When all thirteen gates pass, the factory merges (merge commit) and the lane moves on. If the merge is refused, it hands the PR to you (see Ready to merge).

docs.title: Real data
docs.text: CLAUDE.md sets how far agents may read real data (never by default): see Real data.

docs.title: Urgency triage
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md has a Release phase line. In mvp (until a first formal release), only blockers are fixed in a PR:

  • the main path breaks on realistic input;
  • private data leaks on realistic input;
  • a hard rule is violated;
  • irreversible loss or overwrite of the user's existing data (source files, history, remote repos) on a plausible invocation, even a mistaken one, when a cheap guard would prevent it;
  • a test falsely passes.

Everything else goes into one improvement issue per PR, usually in a hardening lane. Set the line to hardening before a release, and reviews become thorough again.

docs.title: Docs ship with the code
docs.text: Every code change brings its docs in the same PR: see Docs ship with the code.

docs.title: Real data
docs.text: The first line of the Real data section in CLAUDE.md sets how far agents may go. You choose it with the real_data_access question when you create the project; the skill reads it from main.

docs.title: The three levels
docs.text: Line What agents may do Real data: never (default) Agents do not read real user data. You run shapes-only scripts (record types, field names, counts, never values) and reply with the output. Real data: with-approval Agents may read real data on your machine only after you approve one named data source on the issue or PR, for that issue or PR only. Until then they ask, as a question on the PR. Real data: allowed Agents may read real data on your machine when a task needs it.

docs.title: Rules at every level
docs.text:
• Real data is never committed and never quoted in issues, PRs or commits; only field names, counts and shapes. This includes what factory-lesson files upstream.
  • Tests use synthetic fixtures only.
  • Agents read data where it lives and never copy it into the repo or worktree (a scratch directory outside the repo is fine).
  • A stricter hard rule in CLAUDE.md overrides the level.

docs.title: A missing or malformed line reads as never
docs.text: If CLAUDE.md has no Real data: line, or the value isn't one of the three, the skill treats the repo as never. A repo that adopted just the skill is safe by default.

docs.title: Changing the level
docs.text:
• Copier answer (preferred): uvx copier update --data real_data_access=<level>, in a PR of its own.
  • By hand: edit the Real data: line in CLAUDE.md. .copier-answers.yml then still records the old level, and a later copier update can render the old line back.

sync-root-factory never changes this value; it lists it under "Open". See also real_data_access in the Copier questions.

docs.title: Where knowledge lives
docs.text:
Place Holds Who reads it Issues goals, acceptance criteria, lane structure, priorities, dependencies everyone PRs the diff, the Handoff, review threads, questions and answers everyone .factory/designs/issue-N.md the plan, shipped inside the PR reviewers, future agents CLAUDE.md project context, release phase, real-data access, checks, hard rules every agent, every session lesson issues in amplifactory factory problems found while driving a project the template's next release .factory/runs/ (gitignored) run log: events, timings, token costs, pointers to PRs, commits and threads the orchestrator, for resume and cost Claude Code's memory (~/.claude/projects/…) your preferences, how you like to work your Claude Code sessions on this machine Copilot Memory (on GitHub) facts and preferences Copilot stores as it works; repository memories are shared with everyone who uses Copilot Memory in the repo Copilot sessions. Listed in the repo's Settings > Copilot > Memory, and yours at github.com/settings/copilot/memory. Off in -p runs unless --enable-memory; unused memories expire after 90 days by default (docs)

A preference that is really a project rule belongs in CLAUDE.md, not in memory.

docs.title: The run log only points
docs.text: The run log holds no decisions, only entries like "PR #34 asked a question, thread …" or "issue #4 merged at e24eea1, 410k tokens". If you delete it you lose only the cost history; state is rebuilt from GitHub.

docs.title: The Handoff
docs.text:
Every PR body has a ## Handoff section, which the builder keeps current after every change:

  • what changed and why;
  • key decisions;
  • how to test;
  • what's open.

A fresh session or reviewer starts from it, not from a transcript.

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
The Quick start walks this path with one small project. This page is the reference for each step.

You need:

  • Python 3.9 or newer (the skill's scripts run as python3)
  • uv
  • git
  • the GitHub CLI (gh, logged in)
  • GitHub Copilot (the CLI or the app), or Claude Code

The path is: copier, gh scopes, bootstrap, then Copilot (or Claude Code). The Actions mode comes last and is optional: it's off unless Copier's actions_agent is copilot or claude.

docs.title: 1. Generate the repo
docs.text:
uvx copier copy gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory my-project

Copier 9.5 or newer is required (uvx fetches the latest).

Copier asks a few questions: the project and package names, a description, what the agents should know about the project, project-specific hard rules, Python versions, the release phase, whether agents may read your real data (never by default) and whether to add the GitHub Actions mode (actions_agent, none by default). Defaults are filled in; project_name defaults to the destination folder's name, kebab-cased. If the folder name differs from the project name (My Project becomes my-project), the closing message says which repo bootstrap will create.

Private fork

The template repo is public, so Copier needs no credentials. If you copy from a private fork, Copier needs your GitHub credentials: run gh auth setup-git so the gh: shortcut (HTTPS) uses your gh login, or use the fork's git@github.com:… URL.

docs.title: 2. Give gh the scopes it needs
docs.text:
gh auth refresh -h github.com -s repo,workflow,project
  • repo: creating the repo and pushing to it.
  • workflow: pushing a repo that contains GitHub Actions workflows.
  • project: the factory's Project board (bootstrap and lanes.py project-add).

docs.title: 3. Run the bootstrap
docs.text:
cd my-project
./scripts/bootstrap.sh --public      # or --private

bootstrap.sh does what a template can't. It's safe to re-run:

Step What it does Lockfile and first commit uv lock, then git init and the first commit GitHub repo creates and pushes it (--public or --private). For a repo that already exists, it pushes main only when your local main is ahead of origin/main, and stops if they have diverged (git pull --rebase, then re-run) Labels the factory labels, improvement, lane, P0–P3 and documentation Documentation tech-debt issue the tracking issue whose sub-issues are documentation todos (labels documentation, P2) Ruleset protecting main no deletion or force push; PRs need 1 approval and code-owner review; all conversations resolved; required checks Tests (Python X) and Lint; admins can bypass for PRs only Fork PRs workflows from outside contributors need your approval Project board "<project> factory", linked to the repo, with a Priority field

Rulesets need a public repo or GitHub Pro

On GitHub Free, rulesets aren't enforced on private repos. Then main isn't protected, and the script says so. Enterprise managed user (EMU) accounts, such as a work account, can create only private repos in their own namespace, so they use --private. Whether rulesets apply to those repos is unverified; the script warns if GitHub refuses one.

docs.title: 4. Start GitHub Copilot or Claude Code
docs.text:
copilot         # GitHub Copilot CLI, or open the repo in the Copilot app
claude          # or Claude Code

The factory skill works from here and needs no secret: it runs in your session, on the orchestrator model from CLAUDE.md → "Models". Continue with your first run.

docs.title: 5. Optional, last: the Actions mode
docs.text:
The Actions mode runs agents on GitHub Actions when you add labels. It's off by default: generate with --data actions_agent=copilot or --data actions_agent=claude, or add it later with uvx copier update --data actions_agent=…, in a PR of its own.

With Copilot (copilot), the agents are the GitHub Copilot CLI, signed in with each workflow's own token: no secret, and their requests bill your Copilot seat. Bootstrap lets workflows open pull requests, which the agents need; if you add the mode later with copier update, run the command the update prints instead. Where GitHub-hosted runners are off (EMU accounts), set up the runner pool first, so FACTORY_RUNNER is local: the agents then run on your Mac, like CI.

With Claude (claude), the agents are Claude Code GitHub Actions, so this mode needs a Claude subscription, the Claude GitHub App and a token secret. Then:

  1. In Claude Code, run /install-github-app, pick the repo, and choose your subscription. That saves CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN.
  2. Close the PR the installer opens (claude.yml, claude-code-review.yml). The template's factory-chat.yml and factory-review.yml already cover those, with sender and fork checks.

docs.title: What a generated repo contains
docs.text: Path Purpose CLAUDE.md Agent guide: project context, release phase, real-data access, each role's model for Copilot and Claude Code, "checks pass" definition (identical to CI), hard rules .claude/skills/factory/ The factory skill: SKILL.md, references/ (subagent briefs, merge gates, issue and lane format), scripts/queue.py (lane-aware queue), scripts/lanes.py (lanes, sub-issues, dependencies, priorities, Project board, the Documentation tech-debt issue), scripts/runlog.py (run log) .claude/commands/ Stage prompts: design-issue, build-from-design, review-against-design (used by both modes) .github/workflows/factory-*.yml Only with an Actions mode: design, build, review and the label guard; with actions_agent: claude, chat (@claude) too .github/workflows/ci.yml Tests on each Python version, pinned ruff format and lint; on your Mac's runner pool when FACTORY_RUNNER is local, skipped for drafts and when FACTORY_CI is off (CI variables) .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/factory-task.yml Factory task template (never auto-applies factory:design) .github/CODEOWNERS You own every file, so with the "Protect main" ruleset each PR needs your approval .factory/designs/ Plans, shipped inside each implementation PR .factory/runs/ The skill's run log: a local cache and cost ledger pointing at PRs, commits and threads (gitignored) pyproject.toml, package, tests/ Minimal uv/hatchling skeleton so the checks run from day one scripts/bootstrap.sh One-time GitHub setup (above)

docs.title: Your first run
docs.text:
The Quick start runs this on one small project. This page explains each step.

Start GitHub Copilot or Claude Code from inside the repo, so it loads the repo's CLAUDE.md and the factory skill, and check that it's on the orchestrator model (CLAUDE.md → "Models"; Claude Opus by default):

cd my-project
copilot         # GitHub Copilot CLI; then /model to confirm claude-opus-5.5
claude          # or Claude Code; then /model to confirm opus

In the GitHub Copilot app, start a session in the repo's folder.

docs.title: 0. Check bootstrap's output
docs.text:
Before you start, confirm ./scripts/bootstrap.sh finished cleanly (it's safe to re-run):

  • The factory labels exist in the repo, including improvement, lane, P0–P3 and documentation.
  • The Project board "<project> factory" exists, is linked to the repo and has a Priority field (P0–P3). If bootstrap said the board was skipped, run gh auth refresh -h github.com -s project and re-run it.
  • The "Documentation tech-debt" tracking issue exists.
  • On a private repo, look for the ruleset warning: on GitHub Free, rulesets aren't enforced on private repos, so main isn't protected. Make the repo public or use GitHub Pro if you want the protection. EMU (work) accounts can only create private repos; whether rulesets apply there is unverified, so check for the warning.

CI on your Mac. CI runs on GitHub-hosted runners unless you opt in to a runner pool on your Mac. Where they're off (EMU personal repos, for one), say "set up CI runners". It's a few questions: how many jobs run at once, whether to install the pool's login service, and whether to send this repo's CI to it. Then one CI run proves it works. This happens once per Mac and once per repo. See Local CI setup.

docs.title: 1. Brainstorm into lanes
docs.text:
brainstorm a CLI that converts session logs into a dataset into issues

The orchestrator talks it through with you: goals, constraints, what's out of scope, and how you'll know it works. Then it proposes lanes: features with a priority (P0–P3) and dependencies between them. Inside each lane are the ordered issues. Only the next one or two per lane are written in full; the rest are stubs. You'll see a table like this:

Lane Priority Issues, in order Depends on A: core conversion P0 reader → writer + CLI — B: dataset builder P1 export → builder → validation — C: hardening P3 edge cases… lane A

Confirm once. It creates the lane issues, their sub-issues in order, the "blocked by" links, the priority labels and the Project board items. See Lanes and priorities.

docs.title: 2. Run the factory
docs.text:
run the factory

  1. queue.py shows each lane's current issue and "Work now". If several lanes are ready, it asks you whether to run them in parallel. The default is one lane.
  2. A builder writes the plan (.factory/designs/issue-N.md) and opens a draft PR from a local/issue-N branch.
  3. The orchestrator checks the plan. For a critical issue (privacy or security code, a new dependency, a shared data contract), a fresh design reviewer does it.
  4. The same builder builds, updates the docs the change affects, fills in the PR's Handoff (with its Docs line), and marks the PR ready.
  5. A fresh reviewer posts inline comments tagged [blocker], [improvement], [doc-debt] or [question], while CI runs. Docs that disagree with the PR's code are a blocker.
  6. The builder fixes blockers. Improvements become one improvement issue; doc-debt findings become sub-issues of the "Documentation tech-debt" issue.
  7. When every gate passes, including all review threads resolved, the orchestrator merges. The lane moves to its next issue. If the merge is refused, the PR is labelled factory:ready-to-merge with the merge command in a comment, and you merge it (details).

docs.title: 3. When it needs you
docs.text:
You'll see a question on the PR with options and a recommendation, and the label factory:needs-maintainer. Only that lane pauses. Reply in the thread whenever it suits you, then:

resume the factory

See Flag and continue.

docs.title: 4. At the end
docs.text: The run summary lists what was merged, what's waiting on you, which improvements were filed, and the time and token cost per issue (scripts/runlog.py summary). Start a fresh session every two or three issues: GitHub and the run log let it pick up where the last one stopped.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
You'll create a private project from amplifactory, put its CI on your Mac's runner pool, turn one small idea into issues and let the factory take them to merged PRs. The example is slugify, a CLI that turns a title into a URL slug. It's offline, stdlib only and has trivial tests. It takes about 20 minutes plus the factory's run time.

The commands and output below are from a real run of this path on macOS with a GitHub Enterprise Managed User (EMU) account, where hosted runners are off. Names are swapped for slugify-demo.

docs.title: 0. Check your tools
docs.text:
python3 --version          # 3.9 or newer
uv --version
git --version
gh auth status             # logged in to github.com
copilot --version          # GitHub Copilot CLI (or use the Copilot app)

Where GitHub-hosted runners are off

That is the case for EMU personal repos. CI then needs the runner pool on your Mac. Step 4 sets it up from inside Copilot. If your account has hosted runners, skip step 4: CI runs on ubuntu-latest.

docs.title: 1. Generate the project
docs.text:
cd ~/scratch        # anywhere that is not inside another git repo
uvx copier copy gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory slugify-demo

Copier uses the newest release tag. To pin one, add --vcs-ref vX.Y.Z. Press Enter for the defaults, except:

Question Answer project_name Enter: it defaults to the folder name, slugify-demo. The GitHub repo gets this name cli_name slugify description Turn a title into a URL slug. agent_context A tiny offline CLI that turns a title into a URL slug.

Set maintainer_github to your GitHub login: it is the only login the workflows obey (the default is the template author's). Set author_name, author_email and homepage to yours too. All the questions are in Copier questions.

It ends with Generated slugify-demo. and the next steps. Check what it recorded:

cd slugify-demo
grep -E "_src_path|_commit|maintainer_github" .copier-answers.yml

_commit: vX.Y.Z
_src_path: gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory
maintainer_github: <you>

docs.title: 2. Give gh its scopes
docs.text:
gh auth refresh -h github.com -s repo,workflow,project

It changes nothing if your token already has them.

docs.title: 3. Bootstrap, private
docs.text:
./scripts/bootstrap.sh --private

It creates the GitHub repo, the labels, the "Documentation tech-debt" issue, the ruleset protecting main and the Project board. It's safe to re-run. Check it:

gh repo view <you>/slugify-demo --json visibility,url
gh issue list -R <you>/slugify-demo          # #1 Documentation tech-debt
gh api repos/<you>/slugify-demo/rulesets --jq '.[] | .name + " " + .enforcement'

Protect main active

If bootstrap warns that it couldn't create the ruleset, main is unprotected: see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 4. Start Copilot and set CI up on the pool
docs.text:
copilot       # in slugify-demo; /model should show claude-opus-5.5, the orchestrator in CLAUDE.md

Say set up CI runners. The factory-ci skill sets up the pool (it is opt-in; "run the factory" only checks it afterwards). It asks before each step: the repo setting for Actions, how many jobs may run at once, installing the pool's login service (once per Mac), pointing this repo at it, and one smoke-test CI run. Details: Local CI setup.

Check it from a normal terminal:

gh variable list -R <you>/slugify-demo
python3 .claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/setup.py doctor --repo <you>/slugify-demo

FACTORY_RUNNER  local
ok: FACTORY_RUNNER is local
ok: the pool serves this repo
ok: actions/runner 2.338.2 installed
ok: the pool is up (0/8 busy)

docs.title: 5. Brainstorm into lanes
docs.text:
In the same session:

brainstorm a CLI that turns a title into a URL slug into issues

Answer its questions briefly: offline, standard library only, slugify "Hello, World!" prints hello-world, ASCII is enough. It proposes a lane of ordered issues and asks you to confirm once. Then it creates them. From the run:

python3 .claude/skills/factory/scripts/queue.py

  lane  pri  state     current    then              title
    #2  P0   ready     #3         #4                Title to URL slug CLI

Lanes in parallel: 1
Work now: lane #2 → #3 (ready)
Paused, waiting on the maintainer: none

CI pool: up, 0/8 busy, 0 queued

Lane #2 holds #3, "Define and test the title-to-slug conversion contract", then #4, "Expose title-to-slug conversion through the CLI". See Lanes and priorities.

docs.title: 6. Run the factory
docs.text:
run the factory

For each issue, in order: a builder writes the plan and opens a draft PR from local/issue-N, then builds and marks it ready. CI runs on the pool while a fresh reviewer comments inline. The builder fixes the blockers, and the orchestrator merges when every gate passes. Watch from a second terminal:

gh pr list -R <you>/slugify-demo --state all
gh run list -R <you>/slugify-demo

If it asks you something, it's a PR comment with options and the label factory:needs-maintainer. Answer in the thread and say resume the factory. If it can't merge, the PR gets factory:ready-to-merge and a merge command in a comment: run it. See Flag and continue.

When it's done:

git pull
uv run slugify "Hello, World!"      # hello-world

docs.title: 7. What the factory keeps
docs.text:
The run log, .factory/runs/<date>.jsonl (gitignored), holds one line per orchestrator step: the plan, review and merge for each issue, with timings, tokens and pointers to PRs and commits. It holds no decisions. GitHub does, so deleting the log loses only the cost history.

python3 .claude/skills/factory/scripts/runlog.py status     # last step per issue
python3 .claude/skills/factory/scripts/runlog.py summary    # wall time, fix rounds and tokens per issue

#3: done (last step: merge at 2026-11-27T07:38:21+00:00)
 issue      wall  fixes  tokens by model | by role
    #3       0m      0  claude-opus-5.5=52,000, claude-sonnet-5.5=38,000 | builder=38,000, reviewer=52,000

(The numbers above are example entries.) A new session picks up from the log and GitHub: say resume the factory. Start a fresh session every two or three issues.

docs.title: 8. Found a factory problem? File a lesson
docs.text:
If the factory itself got something wrong (a bad default, a skill that misleads the agent, a gate that blocks a good PR) and not your project's code, say it when it happens:

file a factory lesson: the builder skipped the Docs line in the Handoff

The factory-lesson skill drafts an issue, checks it for private data, asks you once and files it with the lesson label in rahmansunny071/amplifactory (the template's repo), never in your own project. A later release fixes it, and sync-root-factory brings the fix into your project. See Lessons.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Day-to-day: the phrases you'll use, and what the factory does on each.
  • Your first run: the pipeline step by step, and what to expect from each one.
  • Create a project: what bootstrap does, the optional Actions mode, what a repo contains.
  • Adopt in an existing repo: add the factory to a repo you already have.

docs.title: Option 1: the whole template
docs.text:
Run Copier into the repo. It shows a conflict for every file that already exists.

cd existing-repo
uvx copier copy gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory .
  • Keep your own pyproject.toml, package and tests where they conflict.
  • Take CLAUDE.md, .claude/, .factory/, .github/ and scripts/bootstrap.sh from the template.
  • Merge your CI into ci.yml and the "checks pass" list in CLAUDE.md; they must stay identical.
  • Run ./scripts/bootstrap.sh. It skips what already exists.

Later releases come in with uvx copier update.

docs.title: Option 2: just the skill
docs.text:
For a repo with no factory skill yet. If you already have factory/, see Keep up to date instead.

URL=gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory; TAG=vX.Y.Z   # a release tag
T=$(mktemp -d)                                  # outside the repo
git init -q --bare "$T/src"
git --git-dir="$T/src" fetch -q --depth 1 "$URL" "refs/tags/${TAG}:refs/tags/${TAG}"
test "$(git --git-dir="$T/src" cat-file -t "refs/tags/$TAG")" = tag || { echo "not annotated: stop"; false; }  # must be tag
git --git-dir="$T/src" archive "$TAG" template/.claude/skills | tar -x -k --strip-components=2 -C .claude/
  • Use a release tag, never main; the skill refuses anything else.
  • Releases up to v0.7.0 have no sync-root-factory; use the first release that ships it.
  • tar -k keeps files you already have, so a same-named skill is not overwritten.
  • Commit the result.

Then add to your CLAUDE.md:

  • Release phase: mvp or hardening, and the blocker definition;
  • Real data: first line Real data: never. (or with-approval / allowed); without it the skill assumes never;
  • Models: the model for each role (orchestrator, builder, reviewer) in Claude Code and GitHub Copilot, copied from the template's CLAUDE.md.jinja; without it the skill uses the template's defaults;
  • "checks pass": a list identical to your CI;
  • Hard rules you want enforced (see CLAUDE.md.jinja), including "every code change ships its docs in the same PR";
  • Where knowledge lives.

Create the labels the skill uses: factory:needs-maintainer, factory:ready-to-merge, improvement, lane, P0 to P3, documentation. The skill creates the "Documentation tech-debt" issue itself when needed.

To update later, see Keep up to date.

docs.title: Organise existing issues into lanes
docs.text:
organise the open issues into lanes

The orchestrator proposes lanes, an order and priorities; after you confirm, it wires them with lanes.py.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot and Claude Code
docs.text:
The factory runs in GitHub Copilot (the CLI or the app) or in Claude Code. A generated repo has one set of files for both: the factory skill, the stage prompts in .claude/commands/ and CLAUDE.md. Each harness reads them. What differs is the tool names, the permission system, the model names and the memory.

Pick one per session. You can use both on the same repo, one after the other: the state lives on GitHub and in the repo, not in the session (Where knowledge lives).

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
You need Python 3.9+, uv, git and gh (logged in), plus one harness:

GitHub CopilotClaude Code 
copilot --version     # the Copilot CLI; or open the project in the Copilot app

Sign in once with the CLI's login command. Copilot needs an active Copilot plan. An organization's policy can limit the models on offer.

claude --version

Claude Code needs a Claude subscription or API access.

Then generate and bootstrap the project as in the Quick start, and start the harness in the project folder (copilot or claude). Say brainstorm X into issues, then run the factory. Where hosted runners are off, say set up CI runners first (Local CI).

Start on the orchestrator's model

Check /model before you start. The orchestrator model is in the generated CLAUDE.md under "Models".

docs.title: What works where
docs.text:
What GitHub Copilot Claude Code The factory, factory-ci, factory-lesson and sync-root-factory skills (.claude/skills/) Yes: say what you want ("run the factory", "set up CI runners", "file a factory lesson: …", "sync the factory") Yes, the same phrases The stage prompts /design-issue N, /build-from-design N, /review-against-design PR (.claude/commands/) Yes, as slash commands (the Actions mode runs them with copilot -p) Yes CLAUDE.md (project rules, models, checks) Read by the session. Subagents don't load it on their own, so each brief tells them to read it Read by the session and its subagents Helper scripts (queue.py, lanes.py, runlog.py, setup.py, sync.py) Yes: plain Python, run from the shell Yes Letting the skill merge by itself A personal permissionRequest hook running merge_hook.py A permissions.allow rule in settings.json

The helper scripts are the same everywhere. See Scripts.

docs.title: Which model for which role
docs.text:
The factory gives each role its own model and passes it explicitly when it spawns the role. The names differ by harness. The generated CLAUDE.md has this table under "Models", and you can edit it:

Role Claude Code GitHub Copilot Orchestrator: your session; plans lanes, checks plans, runs the gates, merges opus claude-opus-5.5 Builder: plans, builds and fixes one issue (also the resume builder and issue writers) sonnet claude-sonnet-5.5 Reviewer: design and code reviewer, fresh for each issue opus claude-opus-5.5
  • /model shows and changes the session's model in both.
  • The builder is the cheap role and the orchestrator and reviewer are the careful ones. A fresh reviewer per issue has no memory of how the builder reasoned, which is what makes the review independent.
  • If a role's model isn't available to you, the factory uses the closest one that is and says so in its run summary.
  • The Actions mode sets its own model: agent_model (Claude, default sonnet) or copilot_model (Copilot, default claude-sonnet-5.5). See Copier questions.

docs.title: What differs
docs.text:
GitHub Copilot Claude Code Spawn a role with a model the task tool with agent_type: "general-purpose" and model:; the builder in the background a subagent with model: set Message the same builder again write_agent SendMessage Read a subagent's result read_agent, after it finishes its final message Ask you a question in the session ask_user. In autopilot and -p runs nobody answers: the factory takes the safe default or flags the question on the PR AskUserQuestion Permissions its own tool rules and approval prompts, and hooks permissions rules in settings.json, and permission modes Memory Copilot Memory, hosted on GitHub; repository memories are shared with everyone who uses it in that repo local and private, under ~/.claude/projects/…/memory

The skill's "Claude Code and Copilot" section maps every action to both tool sets, so the same steps run in each.

Memory is a pointer, not a record. Decisions, plans, handoffs and lessons live on GitHub and in the repo. A preference that is really a project rule belongs in CLAUDE.md. When memory and GitHub disagree, GitHub wins.

docs.title: Permissions and merging
docs.text:
Neither harness may merge on its own unless you opt in, and the template ships no opt-in. When the gates pass but the merge is refused, the PR gets factory:ready-to-merge and a comment with the exact command, and the lane moves on.

  • Claude Code: one allow rule for gh pr merge * --merge --admin --delete-branch.
  • Copilot: the Claude rule does nothing there, and a blanket gh pr allow would also approve gh pr close. Use the personal hook that runs merge_hook.py, which approves only the factory's exact merge command.

Both are in Flag and continue: Let the factory merge.

docs.title: The GitHub Actions mode, with Claude or with Copilot
docs.text:
The optional Actions mode runs design, build and review agents on GitHub Actions when you add labels. Copier's actions_agent question picks the agent: none (default), claude or copilot.

actions_agent: claude actions_agent: copilot Agent Claude Code GitHub Actions the GitHub Copilot CLI, installed per job at a pinned version Sign-in a Claude subscription: /install-github-app in Claude Code, which creates the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN secret none: each workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN signs in (copilot-requests: write) Bills your Claude subscription the repo owner's Copilot seat Model agent_model copilot_model Workflows design, build, review, chat, label guard design, build, review, label guard @claude chat on a PR yes (factory-chat.yml) no: edit the design branch yourself Tool limits an --allowedTools list per stage a preToolUse hook (tool_rules.py) installed from the default branch, with a self-check that fails the job if it doesn't deny PRs opened by a workflow work as is need "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" (bootstrap turns it on); an approve-runs job approves the held CI runs Runners ubuntu-latest your Mac's runner pool when FACTORY_RUNNER=local and the repo is private, else ubuntu-latest

Switch, add or remove it in a PR of its own:

uvx copier update --data actions_agent=copilot   # or claude, or none

The skill and the Actions mode don't start each other: the skill never adds trigger labels and works on local/issue-N branches, while the Actions review takes only factory/issue-*. Use one per issue.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Copilot says it can't find the skill or the commands: start it in the project root, where .claude/ is.
  • A role runs on the wrong model: check /model, then the "Models" table in CLAUDE.md.
  • ask_user returns "user not available": you are in autopilot or a -p run. Ask the question again in a normal session, or answer on the PR.
  • More in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Day-to-day
docs.text:
Start GitHub Copilot or Claude Code from the repo's folder, on the orchestrator model (CLAUDE.md, "Models"; Claude Opus by default).

You say What happens "brainstorm X into issues" Lanes, then ordered issues. You confirm once; everything is created and wired. "run the factory" queue.py picks the work; issues go plan, build, review, merge, lane by lane. "run lanes A and B in parallel" Raises the lane limit for this run (otherwise it asks when more lanes are ready). "resume the factory" Replied questions first, then in-flight issues from the run log, then new work. "what's the factory doing?" queue.py plus runlog.py status: lanes, current issues, what waits on you. "how much did that cost?" runlog.py summary: wall time, fix rounds and tokens by model, per issue. "move #9 before #8" lanes.py order; the lane runs in the new order.

docs.title: On GitHub
docs.text:
• Answer questions in PR threads labelled factory:needs-maintainer, then say "resume".
  • Merge PRs the factory won't: anything touching .github/, CLAUDE.md or .claude/.
  • Triage improvement issues when a lane finishes: prioritise, add to a hardening lane, or close.
  • Check the Project board, grouped by Parent issue.

docs.title: Keep sessions small
docs.text: Start a fresh session every two or three issues. GitHub and the run log hold the state; "resume the factory" rebuilds the picture.

docs.title: Before a release
docs.text: Set CLAUDE.md's Release phase to hardening, in its own PR that you merge. Reviews become thorough, and improvements are fixed in the PR instead of filed.

docs.title: Evolving the template
docs.text: Flow: file a lesson, release, projects update.

docs.title: 1. File a lesson
docs.text: File it when it happens: say "file a factory lesson: ..." in a generated repo. See Keep up to date.

docs.title: 2. Release
docs.text:
1. Open a branch release/vX.Y.Z and a PR that closes the lessons.
  2. Add a CHANGELOG.md entry saying what changed and why, and set template/.claude/skills/factory/VERSION to X.Y.Z. Rename the Unreleased entry to vX.Y.Z (date) in the same commit as the bump; the version check in scripts/check.sh compares VERSION with the first - vX.Y.Z bullet.
  3. Template CI is green on the PR and scripts/check.sh passes locally. Both render every variant in .github/workflows/template-ci.yml, run each generated project's checks, and assert every guardrail.
  4. Merge, then tag vX.Y.Z. Copier only sees tags.

docs.title: 3. Update projects
docs.text: Projects pick the release up with copier update or the sync-root-factory skill. See Keep up to date.

docs.title: Develop the template
docs.text:
• Start with the repo's root CLAUDE.md (layout, release procedure, hard rules). It never ships.
  • Run the local "checks pass" with scripts/check.sh (commit first). It runs the variants in parallel (-j N or CHECK_JOBS; -h for usage), and scripts/test-check.sh tests it (Template CI job check-sh, on Ubuntu and macOS). The skill scripts' --self-test runs are listed in CLAUDE.md.
  • Template files live in template/; files ending in .jinja are rendered.
  • Copier uses [[ ... ]] and [% ... %], so GitHub Actions ${{ ... }} stays untouched.
  • The guardrail check scans rendered files for leftover template syntax. Avoid look-alike sequences in Python, such as two closing square brackets in a row; use type aliases.
  • To render the working tree instead of the latest tag, use --vcs-ref HEAD.
  • The docs in docs/ are the source of the docs site (GitHub Pages). .github/workflows/docs.yml publishes them on every push to main that touches the docs.

docs.title: Keep up to date
docs.text: Both skills run in GitHub Copilot or Claude Code inside your project: sync-root-factory brings in releases, factory-lesson files factory problems upstream.

docs.title: Update a generated repo
docs.text:
Copier records the version in .copier-answers.yml. Run uvx copier update, or say "sync the factory to the latest release". The skill opens a PR for you to merge; it never merges.

  • Before copier update, sync.py copier-check <tag> confirms the tag is annotated, _commit is a release tag, and _src_path is the GitHub template (not a local clone).
  • Copier does a three-way merge and marks conflicts. The skill resolves the mechanical ones and lists the rest.
  • Tags come from the template _src_path names: gh:rahmansunny071/amplifactory, or the old gh:rahmansunny071/agent-factory (it still works and means the same repo).

docs.title: Update a repo that only carries the skill
docs.text:
A repo that adopted only the factory/ skill (see Adopt in an existing repo) has no .copier-answers.yml. .claude/skills/factory/VERSION records the release the copy came from. Say "sync the factory to the latest release". The skill:

  • works on a new branch local/adopt-<tag> cut from a fresh origin/<default branch>, and refuses a dirty tree;
  • replaces every skill folder the tag ships (factory/, factory-lesson/, sync-root-factory/, ...) byte for byte from the tag. A folder the old tag had is replaced only after it matches the version the repo claims. A new folder is added. A folder the old tag did not have but you already have (your own skill, a hand copy) is refused, never overwritten. Your other skills are never touched;
  • turns the CHANGELOG entries since your version into a checklist. It edits CLAUDE.md, .claude/commands/*, README.md and CHANGELOG.md for the ports it can do safely, never sets a policy value (the Real data: level, the release phase), creates only missing labels, and lists everything else under "Open";
  • opens a PR with a Handoff and never merges it.

Every sync, the first included, runs the target tag's sync.py, extracted outside the repo. Never run the copy in the repo: it may predate the guards, and on the first sync it does not exist. Nothing is committed before the adopt branch exists, so this works on a protected main.

R=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel); TAG=vX.Y.Z  # latest release
URL=https://github.com/rahmansunny071/amplifactory.git
gitc() { GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 git -c 'credential.helper=!gh auth git-credential' "$@"; }  # gh's token, for a repo git can't read anonymously
T=$(mktemp -d)                                  # outside the repo
git init -q --bare "$T/src"
gitc --git-dir="$T/src" fetch -q --depth 1 "$URL" "refs/tags/${TAG}:refs/tags/${TAG}"
git --git-dir="$T/src" cat-file -t "refs/tags/$TAG"    # must print: tag  (annotated)
mkdir "$T/x" && git --git-dir="$T/src" archive "$TAG" template/.claude/skills/sync-root-factory | tar -x -C "$T/x"
python3 -I "$T/x/template/.claude/skills/sync-root-factory/scripts/sync.py" --repo "$R" status
# first sync only, while factory/VERSION is missing: add --assume-tag <tag the folder was copied from>
  • --assume-tag stands in for the missing factory/VERSION on the first sync; the folder is still checked against that tag. Leave it out later; sync.py refuses one that disagrees with VERSION.
  • Then ask the agent to sync; it runs the same extracted script.
  • Do not copy sync-root-factory/ into the repo and commit it: the adopt branch is cut from origin/<default>, which would not contain it. If you did and the old tag did not ship it (before v0.8.0), apply refuses it. On local/adopt-<tag>, run git rm -r .claude/skills/sync-root-factory, commit, and rerun.

docs.title: If the check fails
docs.text:
If your copy matches no tag (for example a main-only commit on top of a tag), the sync stops and lists the differing files. There is no override.

  • Edits wanted: port them after the sync.
  • Edits unwanted: on local/adopt-<target tag> (a commit on local main is not on that branch), restore the recorded tag: the version in factory/VERSION or your --assume-tag, not the target tag. Then rerun the sync.
OLD=v0.7.0                                      # the recorded tag
git init -q --bare "$T/old"
git --git-dir="$T/old" fetch -q --depth 1 "$URL" "refs/tags/${OLD}:refs/tags/${OLD}"
test "$(git --git-dir="$T/old" cat-file -t "refs/tags/$OLD")" = tag || { echo "not annotated: stop"; false; }
rm -rf "$R/.claude/skills/factory"
git --git-dir="$T/old" archive "$OLD" template/.claude/skills/factory | tar -x --strip-components=2 -C "$R/.claude/"
git -C "$R" add -A .claude/skills/factory && git -C "$R" commit -m "restore factory/ to $OLD"

docs.title: File a factory problem upstream
docs.text:
A factory problem (not a bug in the project's own code) is filed in amplifactory as an issue labelled lesson, when it happens, not at the end of the run. It states what happened (with links), the fix applied in the project if any, and the template files to change. See Evolving the template.

In a generated repo, say "file a factory lesson: ...". The factory-lesson skill:

  1. Finds the template repo from _src_path in .copier-answers.yml, only if it is a GitHub source (gh:, https://github.com/, ssh://git@github.com/, git@github.com:). A local path, empty value or missing file falls back to rahmansunny071/amplifactory, the template's own repo. The old slug rahmansunny071/agent-factory (any case) maps to it. It confirms the slug with gh repo view and never files in the current repo.
  2. Searches open and closed lesson issues for a duplicate. An open match gets a comment instead of a new issue. A closed match is already fixed: it points to the fixing release and to updating (copier update or sync-root-factory).
  3. Drafts the body (What happened, Fix applied in the generated repo, Template files to change, Options, Takeaway) and checks it for real data, secrets and private paths, since the issue goes to another repo.
  4. Asks you once. If you edit the draft, it re-checks the text and shows the result before filing. It creates the issue with the lesson label and reports the URL.
  5. Offers a comment on the downstream PR or issue linking the lesson, only if you agree.

It needs a gh login with access to the template repo.

docs.title: Local CI setup
docs.text:
Use this when GitHub-hosted runners are off for your account (EMU personal repos, for example) and a generated repo's CI never starts. The factory-ci skill puts CI on a runner pool on your Mac.

The setup is opt-in. Where GitHub-hosted runners are off, say "set up CI runners". Otherwise CI runs on ubuntu-latest and nothing is asked.

The agent runs setup.py (in .claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/) and asks at each decision. Nothing that changes a repo setting or your Mac happens without your yes. Every step is safe to repeat.

# Step What it asks or does 1 Preflight Checks macOS; git, gh, uv and python3 where the pool's service will look for them (a copy only inside an app or a virtualenv doesn't count); a gh login with the repo scope; admin on the repo. Prints the fix for anything missing 2 Actions on Asks to turn GitHub Actions on, if it's off 3 Self-hosted allowed Registers a probe runner that never starts, then deletes it. If an enterprise policy blocks self-hosted runners, it says so: ask the policy's owner, or set FACTORY_CI=off and gate merges on the local checks 4 Capacity Asks how many jobs may run at once; proposes a number that leaves 4 performance cores and 16 GB of RAM free 5 Install the pool Asks to install actions/runner (checked against its SHA-256) and the login service com.amplifactory.runner-pool 6 Register the repo Makes the pool serve this repo, with your gh login 7 Route CI Asks to set the repo variable FACTORY_RUNNER=local (see CI variables). Warns if the repo is public 8 Smoke test Runs CI once (workflow_dispatch) and reports queue and run time. Runs ci.yml; if your workflow has another name it asks which, and --workflow FILE picks it 9 Retire old runners Lists runners you registered by hand for this repo and asks before removing each. For a local runner service, it gives you the svc.sh commands to stop it

A second repo on the same Mac skips steps 4 and 5.

docs.title: Afterwards
docs.text:
Every "run the factory" starts with setup.py doctor (about a second). It reports one of four states:

  • healthy;
  • setup needed: with FACTORY_RUNNER unset that just means hosted runners, and the factory carries on without asking; with FACTORY_RUNNER=local but no finished pool on this Mac, it tells you once to finish the setup or run gh variable set FACTORY_RUNNER --body github;
  • the pool is down, and it offers to start it (in container mode, a Docker that isn't running counts as down; start Docker Desktop);
  • CI is off.

docs.title: Container mode (optional)
docs.text:
To run each job in its own Linux container instead of on your Mac, say "run CI in containers". It needs Docker Desktop, with about 2 GB of Docker's VM per slot. See Security model for what it keeps out and what it doesn't.

S=.claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/setup.py
python3 $S container check              # Docker, its VM's size, and how to fix them
python3 $S container on --yes           # pulls the image, then restarts the pool
python3 $S container off --yes          # new jobs run on the Mac again

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
S=.claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/setup.py
python3 $S plan --repo OWNER/REPO                       # each step's status and next command
python3 $S apply capacity --repo OWNER/REPO --slots 6
python3 $S apply pool --repo OWNER/REPO --yes
python3 $S apply register --repo OWNER/REPO
python3 $S apply route --repo OWNER/REPO --yes
python3 $S apply smoke --repo OWNER/REPO                # --workflow FILE if CI isn't ci.yml
python3 $S doctor --repo OWNER/REPO

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
• One repo back to GitHub-hosted runners: gh variable set FACTORY_RUNNER --body github.
  • Stop the pool: python3 .claude/skills/factory-ci/scripts/setup.py service uninstall.
  • Remove the pool and its files: ... service uninstall --purge --yes. It deletes only this pool's runner registrations, its containers, and its home, ~/.amplifactory/runner-pool/.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
• v0.17.0 (2026-11-27): The factory runs in GitHub Copilot (#98, #95, #96, #97); an opt-in local CI runner pool (#94, #92, #93); generic fixes (#89, #90, #91, #99, #100, #101); improved docs and a Copilot and Claude Code guide (#55); the docs header shows the release tag (#84); MIT License.
  • #84: the docs header shows the release tag. The repo has tags but no GitHub Releases, so Material's repo widget never showed a version. hooks/release_tag.py reads the newest vN.N tag at build time and a small script adds it, linked, beside the stars and forks.
  • #89: sync-root-factory works with safe.bareRepository=explicit. sync.py passes --git-dir to every git call that reads the shadow clone, and SKILL.md says so, so the skill no longer fails in harnesses (such as GitHub Copilot sessions) that set it.
  • #90: merge gates watch the right run, and stacked PRs move to main first. Gate 1 now means the run for the PR's head commit: "Bounded CI waits" reads headRefOid, finds that commit's run with gh run list --commit, re-reads the head before merging, and on a DIRTY state checks git diff --cached --check. "Merge" starts with "Stacked PRs first": retarget a PR whose base is another PR's branch to main before that branch is merged and deleted, or GitHub closes it. SKILL.md step 8 points at the check.
  • #91: generated ci.yml has one job per Python version. A job-level if: on a matrix job that is skipped posts only its unexpanded name, so required checks such as Tests (Python 3.12) hung. Each version is its own job; every job skips drafts, ready_for_review runs them, and each has a timeout. Template CI checks the rendered file's shape.
  • #99: bootstrap.sh never ends a pipe in grep -q. Under pipefail the writer's SIGPIPE made the 'project' scope check read as missing. grep's output goes to /dev/null instead, and Template CI rejects the pattern.
  • #100: bootstrap.sh doesn't push over an existing origin/main. For an existing repo it fetches origin/main and pushes only when local main is ahead; it reports nothing to push when origin is up to date or ahead, and stops when they have diverged.
  • #101: project_name defaults to the folder name. Copier suggests the destination folder's name, kebab-cased (also when copying into .; _min_copier_version is now 9.5, the first with _folder_name), and the after-copy message names the repo bootstrap.sh will create when the answer differs from the folder. Template CI checks both.
  • scripts/check.sh runs the variants in parallel; scripts/test-check.sh tests it. -j N (or CHECK_JOBS=N) limits the jobs, results print in matrix order, Ctrl-C stops the renders, -h prints the usage, and a repo without mkdocs.yml skips the docs build. scripts/test-check.sh runs it against fake repos, also as Template CI's check-sh job on Ubuntu and macOS (where it also runs under /bin/bash, bash 3.2).
  • #98: the factory skill runs in GitHub Copilot as well as Claude Code (lane #54). SKILL.md has a "Claude Code and Copilot" table that maps each step's tool (sub-agents, write_agent/read_agent, ask_user, long waits), the briefs name roles instead of models, and the generated CLAUDE.md has a "Models" section with the model for each role. Copier's message, bootstrap.sh and the README start with Copilot and keep Claude Code as the alternative. Template CI checks that no line names a Claude-only tool without its Copilot counterpart and that no skill hard-codes a model.
  • #95: an opt-in merge hook for Copilot. Copilot ignores .claude/settings.json, and its tool rules can't allow gh pr merge alone. scripts/merge_hook.py is a permissionRequest hook that approves only gh pr merge <N> --merge [--admin] --delete-branch and leaves everything else to the normal prompt. The README shows how to install it as a personal hook (macOS, Linux and Windows; COPILOT_HOME); the template never ships it, and Template CI checks that.
  • The GitHub Actions mode is a Copier option, off by default. actions_agent is none (no agent workflows), claude (the Claude Code workflows, as before) or copilot. copier update --data actions_agent=… adds it later. The README, CLAUDE.md, bootstrap.sh, the issue template and Copier's message follow the answer, and .github/CODEOWNERS makes the maintainer the owner of every file.
  • #96, #97: Actions mode with Copilot. With actions_agent: copilot, the design, build and review workflows run a pinned, job-local GitHub Copilot CLI signed in with the workflow's own token (copilot-requests: write; no secret), on the model in copilot_model. A hook from the default branch, .github/factory/tool_rules.py, gives each agent only what its Claude twin may do; no agent merges, and the review agent only comments. A design or build run that ends without its PR fails.
